parts.name: Outer jacket
parts.summary: The flexible outer skin protects the cable from everyday wear and holds its layers together.
parts.detail: Jacket material and thickness vary by manufacturer. The outside alone cannot tell you a cable’s data speed.
parts.whatcableDetail: WhatCable checks reported capabilities and connection behaviour; it cannot inspect the physical wiring inside the cable.

parts.name: Shielding
parts.summary: Conductive foil or braid helps reduce unwanted electrical interference.
parts.detail: The outer braid encloses the cable conductors and connects to the metal shell in both plugs. Shell and ground are bonded inside each plug. The high-speed coaxial conductors have their own shields, selectable separately.
parts.whatcable: WhatCable monitors changes in port fault counters during a connection, helping you investigate recurring problems.
parts.whatcableDetail: Repeated connection events can result from movement, unplugging or a connection problem. WhatCable highlights the pattern to help you investigate.

parts.name: Power · VBUS
parts.summary: These conductors carry electrical power from the power source to the receiving device.
parts.detail: USB Power Delivery lets compatible devices negotiate power over the CC connection. Charging depends on the cable, charger and device together. One red path represents a conductor group, not an exact wire count.
parts.whatcable: WhatCable compares the charger’s reported ceiling, the cable’s declared power rating and the negotiated power contract. It distinguishes a cable rating below the charger’s capability from the Mac requesting less, a full battery, charging on hold or a second charger on standby. The negotiated power is the agreed limit for the connection. Actual consumption varies with what the Mac needs.

parts.name: Ground · GND
parts.summary: Ground provides the return path for power and an electrical reference.
parts.detail: Several connector contacts can connect to a shared conductor group. Counting contacts is not the same as counting wires inside the cable.

parts.name: USB 2.0 · D+ / D−
parts.summary: Two wires work together to carry USB 2.0 data.
parts.detail: This pair supports signalling up to 480 Mbps. It remains present in the full-featured example for USB 2.0 connections; it is separate from the high-speed pairs.
parts.whatcable: WhatCable uses the active transport and connected-device information exposed by macOS to explain the connection. For USB 3 hubs, its cable-speed verdict follows the Mac-to-hub uplink rather than a slower link inside the hub. A USB 2.0 peripheral on a faster dock does not by itself establish that the Mac’s cable is slow.

parts.name: Configuration · CC
parts.summary: The configuration channel helps the connected devices establish the connection and negotiate USB Power Delivery.
parts.detail: CC carries control messages rather than your files. The USB-C connection uses it for attachment and orientation detection, power negotiation and communication with cable electronics when present.
parts.whatcable: WhatCable joins the cable identity, partner identity and live connection state rather than treating every report as belonging to the cable. It checks that the connection is active before diagnosing it, helping avoid conclusions based on a retained power contract after unplugging. The result explains what the connected parties agreed to and what may be limiting them.

parts.name: High-speed pairs
parts.summary: Four differential pairs — eight signal conductors — provide the high-speed paths in this full-featured cable.
parts.detail: Four differential pairs use eight coaxial signal conductors here. TX contacts at one plug connect to RX contacts at the other, as shown in the table below. These names identify physical paths; the operating mode controls how they carry data and display traffic. A passive cable qualified for 40 Gbps can support newer PAM-3 signalling with compatible endpoints. This does not upgrade a Thunderbolt 4 port or guarantee the same behaviour for an active cable.
parts.whatcable: WhatCable compares the port, cable and connected device with the negotiated link. It follows available Thunderbolt topology, including the endpoint of an unbranched daisy chain, so a slower downstream device is not automatically blamed on the cable. It can also distinguish macOS accessory blocking from a speed limit. For displays, WhatCable Pro’s Display Diagnostics compares the current resolution and refresh rate with the monitor’s reported modes and the DisplayPort link’s lane count and rate.
parts.whatcableDetail: When macOS does not expose enough information to identify the limiting component, WhatCable shows what is known without guessing. Display Diagnostics also accounts for Display Stream Compression (DSC), so a high-resolution picture carried using compression is not automatically treated as a bandwidth fault.

parts.name: Sideband · SBU1 / SBU2
parts.summary: These two paths support mode-specific auxiliary signalling.
parts.detail: Their role depends on the connection mode. For example, DisplayPort Alt Mode uses them for its AUX channel. They are not the main high-speed data pairs.
parts.whatcable: WhatCable Pro’s Display Diagnostics examines the display link and reported adapter information alongside the monitor’s current mode. This helps explain a screen running below its expected resolution or refresh rate, including connections through HDMI conversion. It reads the reported link state; it does not directly test the individual SBU wires.
parts.whatcableDetail: DisplayPort can train to a lower link rate for the mode currently selected. A lower rate alone does not establish a cable fault: selecting a higher resolution or refresh rate may cause the link to retrain. Adapter details are included when macOS exposes them.

parts.name: E-marker · cable identity
parts.summary: A chip inside the plug tells connected devices what the cable declares it can support. It communicates over CC and receives power through VCONN.
parts.detail: This reference has one e-marker in each plug. Its electrical connections are CC, local VCONN and ground, with Ra termination on VCONN. Full-featured cables require electronic marking, as do USB 2.0 cables above 3 A. Identity electronics do not make the data paths active. The block shows the chip’s function; package dimensions and PCB routing are not a manufacturer layout.
parts.whatcable: WhatCable compares the e-marker’s declared capabilities with the Thunderbolt controller’s reported connection when available. Read those figures together: an older 40 Gbps identity can coexist with a valid 80 Gbps connection when a compatible passive cable carries newer signalling. That difference alone does not establish misreporting. A slower connection may instead reflect the port or device. Pro’s Negotiation Diagnostics shows the per-party figures behind the verdict.
parts.whatcableDetail: A missing vendor ID does not by itself indicate a faulty or counterfeit cable. WhatCable considers it alongside the other identity information. Its trust checks distinguish informational notes from malformed or contradictory capability fields.

parts.name: Coaxial shields
parts.summary: Each of the eight high-speed signal conductors has its own surrounding conductive shield in this coaxial construction.
parts.detail: The shields connect to ground in both plugs. This is the coaxial option in USB-C Table 3-10; separate drain wires are not used. Shielded twisted-pair construction is another option and requires drain connections.

parts.name: VCONN · chip supply
parts.summary: Contact B5 supplies the electronics inside this plug. It is separate from the VBUS conductors that charge your device.
parts.detail: This reference uses an e-marker at each end, as in Figure 4-42. Each chip connects to local B5, CC and ground. No VCONN conductor crosses the cable. A local Ra termination from B5 to ground signals that cable power is needed. The small blocks show electrical functions rather than a specific chip package.
parts.whatcable: If WhatCable cannot show an e-marker, connect a charger, dock or device at the far end and check again: some Macs wait for a connected partner before reading cable identity. Missing data alone does not establish that the chip is absent or broken; availability also depends on the Mac and port.

parts.name: VBUS bypass capacitor
parts.summary: A 10 nF capacitor connects between VBUS and ground inside each full-featured plug.
parts.detail: Table 3-10 specifies a minimum 30 V rating and placement close to the power pad. This reference uses Standard Power Range, not the higher-voltage Extended Power Range. The capacitor is not in series with the charging wires.

basic.name: Basic USB-C
basic.subtitle: USB 2.0 charging & data cable
basic.description: This example is a 3 A USB 2.0 cable without an e-marker. It has power, ground, USB 2.0 and configuration paths, but no high-speed pairs or sideband paths. Other USB 2.0 cables can have e-markers, including those rated above 3 A.

thunderbolt.name: Thunderbolt 4
thunderbolt.subtitle: Passive · 40 Gbps in TB4 operation
thunderbolt.description: Passive reference wiring shown in Thunderbolt 4 operation: eight coaxial high-speed conductors, USB 2.0 D+/D−, CC, two sideband conductors, VBUS and ground. Each plug contains an e-marker, local VCONN supply and Ra termination, plus a 10 nF VBUS bypass capacitor. The opposite plug follows the connection table below. Thunderbolt 4 connections operate at up to 40 Gbps. Compatible passive cables can also carry faster Thunderbolt 5 signalling between compatible endpoints; the TB4 label is not necessarily the cable’s physical speed ceiling.

thunderbolt5.name: Thunderbolt 5
thunderbolt5.subtitle: Passive · 80 / 120 Gbps · up to 240 W
thunderbolt5.description: A short passive, EPR-capable reference: four high-speed differential pairs, USB 2.0, CC, sideband, power and ground. The same signal-path count as our Thunderbolt 4 example supports faster PAM-3 signalling. Each plug has an e-marker and local VCONN supply; the power path and bypass capacitor are rated for Extended Power Range. This illustrates a construction choice, not a teardown of a particular product.

highspeed.summary: Four differential pairs carry Thunderbolt 5 traffic using three-level PAM-3 signalling. The extra speed does not require extra pairs.
highspeed.detail: Normal operation assigns two lanes in each direction for 80 Gbps each way. Bandwidth Boost assigns three lanes towards the display-heavy side and one back, giving 120/40 Gbps. Contact labels in the connection table identify physical wiring, not a fixed operating direction. These are link bandwidths; file-transfer throughput also depends on protocol overhead and devices.

power.summary: This EPR-capable example can carry up to 240 W: 48 V at 5 A, when the charger and receiving device negotiate it.
power.detail: Extended Power Range requires suitable cable insulation, connector construction and voltage-rated components, as well as an EPR-capable e-marker. The current is still 5 A; the higher voltage raises the power ceiling. Thunderbolt data speed and charging power are separate capabilities. A 240 W cable does not force a Mac to draw 240 W. Thunderbolt 4 cables can also support EPR; 100 W is the rating chosen for our TB4 reference, not a universal TB4 limit.
power.sourceLabel: UL Solutions · 240 W EPR cable requirements

marker.detail: This reference retains one e-marker in each plug, powered locally through VCONN. Its identity includes the cable’s supported signalling and EPR capability. An EPR-capable 5 A cable permits charging contracts up to 48 V / 5 A (240 W), when both connected devices support them. The e-marker identifies capabilities; it does not itself generate the faster data signalling.

capacitor.summary: A VBUS-to-ground bypass capacitor sits inside each plug, with a voltage rating suitable for EPR.
capacitor.detail: This reference uses a 10 nF bypass capacitor rated at least 63 V for the EPR power path. The older 30 V minimum described for our SPR example is not suitable here. It connects across VBUS and ground, not in series with charging current. Its illustrated size is not a component footprint.
capacitor.sourceLabel: UL Solutions · EPR bypass capacitor rating

questions.title: Why does it charge but transfer slowly?
questions.text: Charging and data use different conductors. This basic cable has a USB 2.0 pair but no high-speed pairs. WhatCable compares the connection with the port and device capabilities to help identify the limiting link. Switch to Thunderbolt 4 to see the added signal paths.

questions.title: Why isn’t my display at its best mode?
questions.text: Display traffic uses the high-speed paths. WhatCable Pro’s Display Diagnostics compares the current picture, monitor modes and DisplayPort link, including compression and reported adapters. Start by checking the selected resolution and refresh rate; a lower link rate alone does not identify a cable fault.

questions.title: What does the e-marker tell us?
questions.text: The e-marker reports declared capabilities; the controller reports the negotiated connection. A compatible passive cable with an older 40 Gbps identity can legitimately operate at 80 Gbps with newer signalling. A difference is not automatically a false claim. WhatCable presents the available identity and connection evidence to help explain the whole chain. The close-up shows the chip’s connections.

questions.title: How is Thunderbolt 5 faster?
questions.text: The four high-speed pairs stay in place. PAM-3 uses three signal levels to carry more information. Normal operation offers 80 Gbps each way; Bandwidth Boost reallocates one lane to give 120 Gbps towards demanding displays and 40 Gbps back. Compare the bandwidth modes below the model.
